newsitem.title: USA: Witnesses thrown out in cop-killing immigrant case.
newsitem.headline: Witnesses thrown out in cop-killing immigrant case.

text.p: A Texas judge on Monday threw out the testimony of key prosecution witnesses in the case against a Mexican immigrant who was on Death Row for nearly 14 years for the shooting death of a Houston policeman.
But Judge Frank Maloney said he thought prosecutors still had a "prosecutable case" against Ricardo Aldape Guerra and set May 19 as the start date for a new trial.

Aldape Guerra was convicted of shooting officer J.D. Harris in July 1982 during a routine traffic stop. He was sentenced to die by lethal injection and was on Death Row in a Texas prison before his conviction was thrown out by the federal courts last August. He was transferred to county jail.
Aldape Guerra said from the beginning that Harris was shot by Roberto Carrasco Flores, who later died in a police shootout.

In 1994, U.S. District Judge Kenneth Hoyt ordered a new trial after hearings in which he found that police had intimidated witnesses into accusing Aldape Guerra of the shooting and that prosecutors had manipulated evidence in their zeal to convict an alleged cop killer. The ruling was upheld in August by the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals.
Hoyt said police and prosecutors had become "merchants of chaos" by their misdeeds.

Maloney's ruling followed February hearings in which defence attorney Scott Atlas asked that the 1982 indictment be thrown out and the state barred from retrying the case. He also moved that key prosecution witnesses be barred from testifying if there were a new trial.

Maloney agreed that six witnesses who testified against Aldape Guerra in the 1982 trial could not take the stand in a new trial because they had been so influenced by police and prosecutorial misconduct that they were not credible.
"Police did intimidate witnesses by insisting they had seen more than they had seen ... and threatening witnesses with punitive action," Maloney said.
But Maloney refused to throw out the entire case.
"The state still has a prosecutable case even with the suppression of evidence. It's just that I've tried to remove the taint (of misconduct)," he said.
Maloney's rulings may be appealed by either the defence or the prosecution, which could delay a new trial and keep Aldape Guerra in jail.
Or prosecutors, stripped of key witnesses, could drop the case and not retry it, which would allow Aldape Guerra to leave jail and return to Mexico.
"Obviously, that's something that will have to be decided," prosecutor Casey O'Brien told Reuters.
Atlas said the defence wanted to get on with a new trial. "We're not anxious to see Mr. Aldape Guerra remain in jail for one day longer than necessary," he said.
Aldape Guerra originally came to the United State illegally to find work.
